posts.cooked:
English Version

Proposal Update — Revised for Committee Feedback

Corven requests $600 over 4 weeks to add Fiber Network tooling to its working browser-based CKB IDE and test it with Web3 developer clubs across Kenya.

Project Name

Corven: a browser-based IDE for building on CKB and Fiber Network

Team / Individual Profile

  • Name: Jimleston Osoi, Software Engineer
  • Background: Backend developer and data engineer with 5+ years of experience in Node.js, TypeScript, React, PostgreSQL, Redis and AWS. Blockchain experience in Solidity and Go on EVM chains, plus prior work in the Nervos CKB ecosystem through the CKBuilder Program.
  • GitHub: https://github.com/lestonEth
  • Website: https://corvanide.space/
  • Contact: Telegram @lest_ton

Project Description

Problem. Building on CKB, and on Fiber Network in particular, means setting up a local toolchain, running a devnet and nodes, and configuring channels before writing a single line of app code. For new developers, especially students in African Web3 clubs with limited hardware and unreliable internet, this setup is the biggest barrier to entry. Many give up before they ever build.

Solution. Corven is a cloud-native IDE that runs entirely in the browser. Developers open a link and get a ready workspace with a terminal, a private CKB devnet and contract templates, with no local setup. This phase adds Fiber Network to that workspace: running Fiber nodes, opening channels and sending payments from the browser, so new developers can try Fiber in minutes.

Progress so far (CKB foundation, working today):

  • NestJS microservice backend (API gateway, auth, workspace, runtime, file and terminal services) on PostgreSQL and Redis
  • Sign-in with a CKB wallet signature, JWT with refresh-token rotation, and Redis-backed rate limiting
  • Workspaces open in seconds from pre-built templates; scheduling across multiple servers with a shared Rust build cache
  • In-browser editor, terminal, and build and test panels; idle workspaces stop automatically to keep hosting costs down
  • A private CKB devnet for every workspace, started on demand
  • Contract templates with tests: Hello world, a fungible token (sUDT) and a time lock
  • Deploy to the devnet in one click, or to testnet from the developer’s own wallet, with upgradable (Type ID) deployments
  • Transaction debugger with cycle counts and plain-language contract errors
  • Devnet accounts, a cell explorer, a transaction builder and Molecule bindings
  • Built-in browser to preview dApp frontends running in the workspace

Fiber work in progress: a Fiber playground that runs three Fiber nodes (fnn v0.9.1) on the workspace devnet. In local tests the nodes open channels, route a payment through a middle node and close cooperatively. Packaging it into the IDE, with a visual interface, is the first build task of this phase.

Why now. The CKB foundation works. Fiber is the missing piece for our target users, and testing with real developers will show what they need from it. This phase ships the Fiber tooling and tests it in hands-on sessions with Web3 clubs in Kenya.

Website Status and Operational Readiness

[Addresses committee feedback #2]

The committee could not access the previously listed website. The public deployment had been taken offline to avoid hosting costs while the proposal was pending, and the project has since moved to a new domain: https://corvanide.space/.

The project is operational — the full CKB foundation (workspaces, devnet, contract templates, transaction debugger, cell explorer) runs locally and has been demonstrated to testers.

To resolve this before re-review, we will, no later than 3 days after resubmission:

  • Bring up a stable public instance at https://corvanide.space/ with uptime monitoring.

Expected Deliverables

[Addresses committee feedback #1: clear, measurable list of outputs by end of 4-week period]

By the end of the 4-week period (Sunday 8 November 2026), the following outputs will be produced and published. Each is measurable and verifiable.

# Deliverable Measurable Output Where It Will Be Published
1 Fiber playground in Corven A working browser-based Fiber playground, with 3 Fiber nodes (fnn v0.9.1) per workspace, supporting: opening a channel, creating and paying an invoice, and a multi-hop payment routed through a middle node. Verified by a recorded end-to-end test. Live in the Corven IDE at https://corvanide.space/
2 Fiber starter templates 2–3 runnable Fiber starter templates, each with a README, that a new developer can open and run in the browser in under 5 minutes. In the Corven template gallery + public repo
3 Getting-started guide 1 written guide (minimum 1,000 words) covering: opening a workspace, starting Fiber nodes, opening a channel, sending a payment, and deploying a template. Public repo + linked from Corven
4 Open-source code repository Public repo under MIT or Apache-2.0 license containing all Fiber tooling, templates and guide from this phase. GitHub (link to be added)
5 Stable public deployment A public Corven instance that stays online for the full project period and passes a load test of 15–20 concurrent workspaces. https://corvanide.space/
6 3 hands-on testing sessions 3 sessions held in Kisumu, Nairobi and Thika, with a combined minimum of 40 participating developers (attendance logged per session). Sessions + attendance data in the testing report
7 User testing report 1 report containing: participant numbers per session, key feedback themes, a list of bugs found, and the fixes shipped for each. Posted on Nervos Talk + public repo
8 Demo video 1 video (3–5 minutes) showing the Fiber playground in use and the improvements made after each testing session. Public (YouTube / IPFS) + linked on Nervos Talk
9 Final completion report 1 report with a transparent, line-item funding usage breakdown against the $600 budget, plus a summary of deliverables 1–8 and their status. Posted on Nervos Talk

Verification: Each deliverable above will be linked in the final completion report so the committee can independently confirm it was produced. Deliverables #1–#5 are functional artifacts that can be tested directly; #6–#9 are documented evidence of testing and spend.

Testing Plan

[Addresses committee feedback #4: how sessions will be conducted and what feedback will be collected]

Session format (each session, ~3 hours):

Time Activity
0:00–0:20 Intro to CKB and Fiber; what participants will build today
0:20–0:40 Guided signup: each participant opens Corven in the browser, creates a workspace, starts a devnet
0:40–1:30 Hands-on lab A (CKB): compile and deploy a contract template, inspect the transaction in the debugger
1:30–2:15 Hands-on lab B (Fiber): start Fiber nodes, open a channel, create an invoice, send a payment (multi-hop in week 3)
2:15–2:45 Structured feedback collection (survey + short group discussion)
2:45–3:00 Wrap-up, next steps, and how to keep using Corven

What feedback we will collect (and how):

  1. Pre-session baseline survey (Google Form, 5 questions): experience level, prior CKB/Fiber exposure, device and connection type.

  2. Post-session survey (Google Form, 10 questions, 1–5 Likert + open text):

    • Time to first working workspace (minutes)

    • Time to first Fiber payment (minutes)

    • Ease of use of the Fiber playground (1–5)

    • Clarity of the getting-started guide (1–5)

    • Biggest blocker encountered (open text)

    • One feature they would add (open text)

    • Would they use Corven again? (Y/N)

    • Would they recommend it to a club member? (Y/N)

  3. Bug log template completed by facilitators during the session: step to reproduce, expected vs actual, severity.

  4. Session attendance log: names/handles, club, device type, and whether they completed lab A and lab B.

  5. Optional short interviews (3–5 participants per session, 5 minutes each) for qualitative color.

How the evidence will be presented:

  • Raw survey exports (CSV) and the bug log will be published in the public repo alongside the testing report.

  • The testing report will include: participant counts per session, completion rates for each lab, aggregated survey scores (mean + range), a prioritized bug list with fix status, and verbatim quotes (with consent) for qualitative feedback.

  • Screenshots and short clips from each session will be included in the demo video.

Targets: 40+ total participants across the 3 sessions; at least 70% completing lab A and 50% completing lab B; at least 80% answering the post-session survey.

Acceptance Criteria and Evidence Commitments

[Addresses committee feedback #3: concrete, verifiable plans for test data and community feedback]

We acknowledge and accept that if the final report, test data, and community feedback do not meet the committee’s requirements, the project will not be approved for completion. To make this verifiable, we commit to the following:

  1. All raw evidence will be published, not just summaries:

    • Post-session survey exports (CSV, anonymized)

    • Bug log (CSV/Markdown)

    • Attendance logs (anonymized to initials/handles)

    • Pre-session baseline surveys (CSV)

  2. All claims in the final report will be traceable to a specific evidence file or link.

  3. The public deployment will remain online for at least 30 days after the final report, so the committee can independently test the deliverables.

  4. The demo video will show unedited, real-time use of the Fiber playground — not a scripted mockup — so the committee can see the actual product behavior.

  5. If targets are not met (e.g., fewer than 40 participants, or labs not completed), we will report the shortfall honestly and explain the cause, rather than adjust the numbers after the fact.

  6. We will publish weekly progress updates on Nervos Talk (Fridays, weeks 1–3) so the committee can track progress before the final report and raise concerns early.

Required Funding

Total: $600 (equivalent in CKB)

Item Purpose Amount (USD)
Cloud hosting and deployment Servers to run the IDE workspaces, devnets and Fiber nodes during the project period 220
Infrastructure Managed PostgreSQL, Redis, storage, domain and SSL, testnet node 140
Transport and testing logistics Travel to sessions in Kisumu, Nairobi and Thika; mobile data bundles for participants; printed guides 240
Total 600

Estimated Completion Time

4 weeks: Monday 12 October to Sunday 8 November 2026.

To-do List

[Cross-referenced to deliverable numbers so timeline and deliverables link cleanly]

Week 1 (12–18 Oct): Deploy and first session

  • Mon 12: Package the Fiber playground into the IDE (nodes start on the workspace devnet) → Deliverable 1

  • Tue 13 – Wed 14: Deploy the stable public instance at https://corvanide.space/ with monitoring; load-test for 15–20 concurrent workspaces → Deliverables 5, and website status fix

  • Thu 15: Finalise the getting-started guide and the feedback survey; confirm venues and attendee numbers with the clubs → Deliverables 3, 6

  • Fri 16 Oct – Session 1: Kisumu, held alongside the ongoing campus tour (CKB workspace, devnet and contract templates) → Deliverable 6

  • Weekend: Sort feedback and bugs from Kisumu by priority → Deliverable 7

Week 2 (19–25 Oct): Fix and build Fiber

  • Mon 19: Fix the critical bugs and usability issues found in Kisumu → Deliverable 7

  • Tue 20 Oct – Session 2: Web3 clubs in Nairobi → Deliverable 6

  • Wed 21 – Fri 23: Build the Fiber playground interface (network view, channels, invoices and payments) and 2–3 Fiber starter templates; update the guide → Deliverables 1, 2, 3

  • Fri 23: Weekly progress update in the Rock Web5 channel and on Nervos Talk → Acceptance criteria #6

Week 3 (26 Oct – 1 Nov): Fiber session

  • Mon 26 – Tue 27: Fix issues found in Nairobi → Deliverable 7

  • Wed 28 Oct – Session 3: Mount Kenya University (MKU), Thika, focused on the Fiber playground and starter templates → Deliverable 6

  • Thu 29 – Fri 30: Fix issues found at MKU; weekly progress update → Deliverables 7, Acceptance criteria #6

Week 4 (2–8 Nov): Report

  • Publish the user testing report: participants, key feedback, bugs found and fixes shipped → Deliverable 7

  • Record and publish the demo video, including the Fiber playground and the improvements made after testing → Deliverable 8

  • Fri 6 Nov: Submit the completion report with the funding usage breakdown → Deliverable 9

Relevance to the CKB Ecosystem

  • Meets a real ecosystem need: Fiber is CKB’s payment channel network, and growing it depends on more developers building apps on it. Corven removes the setup barrier so new developers can run Fiber nodes and send their first payment from a browser.
  • Grows the developer base in Africa: Testing directly with Kenyan Web3 clubs brings new builders into CKB and creates a feedback loop from an underserved region.
  • Web5 alignment: Corven combines familiar Web2 developer tooling with Web3 infrastructure, and the plan is user-centric: build, test with real users, iterate.
  • Open source: All code is public so other CKB builders can reuse and extend it.

posts.name: 行天春彦
posts.cooked:
Hi @lestonEth,

Thank you for your continued interest in the Spark Program and for submitting the Corven cloud-native IDE proposal.

After review by the Spark Program committee, your proposal has been assigned a status of Pending. This is not a rejection, but an invitation to revise and resubmit.

The committee acknowledges the value of your work — a browser-based IDE that lowers the barrier for new developers to build on CKB is genuinely useful, and the progress you’ve made on the CKB foundation (workspace management, devnet provisioning, contract templates, transaction debugger) is impressive.

Main Revision Recommendations:

  1. Deliverables clarification: Please explicitly state what the expected deliverables and outputs of this phase are. The committee needs a clear, measurable list of what will be produced by the end of the 4-week period.

  2. Website accessibility: The committee was unable to access the provided website (corvan.space). This raises concerns about whether the project is actually operational and can support the proposed activities. Please confirm the website’s status and provide a working link, or explain the current situation.

  3. Acceptance criteria: The committee would like to be clear upfront that if the final report, test data, and community feedback do not meet the committee’s requirements, the project will not be approved for completion. Please ensure your proposal includes concrete — and verifiable — plans for how you will collect and present this evidence.

  4. Testing plan: Since this phase includes hands-on testing with Web3 developer clubs in Kenya, please clarify how the sessions will be conducted and what specific feedback you plan to collect from participants.

Regarding the website being down — if there are hosting issues or recent changes, please let us know. Please revise and resubmit based on the feedback above. We will arrange a new round of review as soon as possible.

Best regards,
xingtian
On behalf of the Spark Program Committee

posts.name: jimleston osoi
posts.cooked:
[Proposal Update]

Hi @xingtianchunyan,thanks to you and the committee for the review.

I’ve revised and resubmitted the proposal to address all four points:

  1. Deliverables — Added a measurable deliverables table (9 outputs, each with a specific metric and publication location), cross-referenced with the to-do list.

  2. Website — Old domain was taken offline to save hosting costs while pending; project moved to https://corvanide.space/.

  3. Acceptance criteria — Added 6 explicit commitments: raw evidence published, 30-day post-report uptime, unedited demo video, honest shortfall reporting. I accept that missing the committee’s requirements means no completion approval.

  4. Testing plan — Added a 3-hour session agenda, 5 feedback instruments, and targets (40+ participants, 70%/50% lab completion, 80% survey response).

Best regards,
lestonEth
